text: Lessons 22 and 23 both assumed JSON shaped as a simple flat list. Real APIs often nest data instead — and that changes everything about how you process it.

Here's what genuinely nested JSON looks like — fare is a whole object, locations has objects inside objects. Hand this straight to a DataFrame, and you get entire dictionaries stuck inside single cells. Not remotely what you want.

JSON dot loads parses JSON text into real Python dictionaries and lists — the same shapes from Lesson 15. Dumps does the reverse. And here's something worth knowing: requests's own dot JSON method, from last lesson, is calling loads for you automatically underneath.

P-D dot JSON normalize is the real fix. It walks every level of nesting and turns it into dot separated column names — fare dot amount, instead of a dictionary sitting inside a fare column. Now it's a real, filterable, summable table.

Flatten it properly, or chain your keys directly when you only need one value. Next lesson: connecting Python to SQL — pulling data straight from a database instead of a file or an API. See you there.
